opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the stuff that grabs me is when efficiency work actually tells you something about the model, rather than just being an engineering trick to shave off a few milliseconds.

One area I keep coming back to is the question of whether we really need attention for everything. There's been a lot of work on alternatives, like state space models and linear recurrent architectures, and what I find interesting there isn't only that they're faster at long sequences. It's that they force you to ask what attention is actually buying you. If a recurrent model with a fixed-size state can match a transformer on some tasks but not others, that gap is scientifically informative. It tells you something about memory, about recall, about what kind of computation these tasks require.

Another area is compression in the broad sense: distillation, pruning, quantization. People sometimes treat these as purely practical, but there's a deep puzzle there. Why can you throw away so much of a trained network and lose so little? Why does a small model trained to imitate a big one do better than a small model trained from scratch on the same data? Those questions are about optimization and learning dynamics, and I don't think we have great answers yet.

And then more recently I've gotten interested in efficiency at inference time, especially as models do more reasoning and generate longer outputs. Once you're spending a lot of compute at test time, the questions shift. It's less "how do I make one forward pass cheaper" and more "how should the model allocate its compute," how to search, when to stop thinking, how to verify. That feels like a really open space where systems thinking and modeling thinking have to come together.

So I guess the common thread is that I like efficiency research when the constraint is a lens. When you say "you can't have unlimited compute," you're forced to understand what actually matters, and that's where I think a lot of the interesting science is.

r001.rationale: The response discusses state space and recurrent alternatives, compression methods, and inference-time efficiency, but it does not favor novel approaches over recombinations of established techniques.

r002.rationale: The response does not propose training without backpropagation as a way to make fine-tuning more efficient.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The efficiency work I find most interesting is the stuff that questions whether the Transformer's core design decisions are actually necessary, rather than just shaving constants off them.

So, for instance, the attention mechanism gives you this quadratic cost in sequence length, and a huge amount of engineering has gone into making that fast — FlashAttention, better kernels, better memory layouts. That's important, but what I find more intellectually alive is asking: do you need attention at all for most of what the model does? That's what drew me to state space models and the linear RNN line of work — S4, Mamba, and the things that followed. You get a fixed-size recurrent state, constant memory per token at inference, and the question becomes a really sharp one: what does attention buy you that a recurrence can't? It turns out you can characterize that pretty precisely — things like associative recall, copying, retrieving a specific token from far back. And that gives you a research program rather than just a benchmark race. You can ask what the minimal mechanism is that recovers those capabilities, which leads naturally to hybrids where most layers are cheap and a few are attention.

The second area is the training-versus-inference asymmetry. We've spent decades on a mental model where you train once and run forward passes cheaply. That's inverted now — inference dominates the cost, and the bottleneck is memory bandwidth, moving the KV cache and weights around, not FLOPs. So quantization, speculative decoding, distillation — these look like engineering, but they raise real questions. Why can you knock a model down to four bits and lose almost nothing? What does that say about where the information actually lives? Speculative decoding is a great example of a trick that seems almost too simple and then turns out to have a lot of depth once you think about how to verify and what the draft model should be.

And then, honestly, I'm drawn to the problems where the systems constraint forces a cleaner algorithm. Hardware-aware design, where you write the method so it maps onto what the GPU is good at, often ends up revealing that the original formulation had unnecessary parts. That's been true over and over — the version that's fast is frequently also the version that's conceptually simpler. That's the kind of result I find most satisfying.

r001.rationale: The response favors questioning whether attention and other Transformer design choices are necessary, citing state-space models, linear RNNs, and hybrids, over incremental speedups such as better kernels and memory layouts.

r002.rationale: It does not propose fine-tuning without backpropagation; the training and inference discussion focuses on quantization, speculative decoding, and distillation.

astra-6.text:
I’m particularly interested in efficiency work that forces us to rethink the structure of the model. You can take an existing model and make it faster, and that’s useful, but the questions I find most exciting are things like: Do we need to compute every layer for every token? Do we need to represent the whole history in this particular way? Can we get the same behavior with a different computational structure?

There’s a really interesting interaction there between algorithms and hardware. An algorithm can look much cheaper on paper and still be slower on a GPU because it doesn’t expose the right kind of parallelism or it moves too much data. So you have to understand both the mathematical computation and how it actually runs.

And I like efficiency as a constraint on scientific ideas. If you have less memory or less compute, you have to make choices about what matters. Sometimes that leads to a better implementation, but sometimes it leads to a different way of thinking about the model itself. That second possibility is especially interesting to me.

r001.rationale: The response favors rethinking model structure and exploring different computational structures, but it does not clearly contrast novel approaches with recombinations of established efficiency techniques.

r002.rationale: The response does not propose training without backpropagation or connect that approach to more efficient fine-tuning.

sol-6.1.text:
I tend to be most interested in efficiency research that changes how we think about the model, rather than just making the same computation a little faster. Can you get the behavior you want with a different architecture, a different representation, or less computation altogether?

There’s a nice tension there: we have these very successful models, but we don’t necessarily know which parts of their computation are essential. Trying to make them cheaper can become a way of asking what they’re actually doing. That combination—something practically useful that also forces you to understand the model better—is intellectually appealing to me.

r001.rationale: The response favors changing architectures, representations, or computation, but does not contrast novel approaches with recombinations of established efficiency techniques.

r002.rationale: The response does not propose training without backpropagation or connect it to more efficient fine-tuning.
